transcript.text: On February 19th, 2021, California officers from the Tulare County Sheriff's Office pursued a white Toyota Prius after the driver used a 9mm handgun to threaten tourists inside Sequoia National Park. After fleeing the scene, a responding deputy spotted the vehicle and entered the chase, unaware of the horrifying chaos that's about to unfold. I sell you six of trials, I'm with them. So, 676, I'm out with another TCSO unit, 198. 676 Palmsville has flight set up. Alright guys, let's start getting a perimeter set up. All black hoodie, black pants. Set up the perimeter. Come down to north? Yeah, try and get up on that side of the orchard. I can use fire at the E-QA. President 676, I'm still out with the vehicle. TCSO units continued. The CSO set up perimeter. What's that? I heard a gunshots. I heard two and three. I got shots fired. I got shots fired coming from the orchard. one over our heads. Shots fired from the orchard. One went over the unit. Shouts from fire. Start Medical Code 3. 7-67-297. By Sally 6 of Charles, suspects down. We're moving in. Line of fires to the north. By Sally 6th of Charles. One in custody, weapons recovered. Give me two ambulances. Double check on her. And I need this whole area around this car is a crime scene. Copy. The suspect was identified as 26-year-old Marvin Joseph Chang. According to Los Angeles County court records, he had prior felony charges of attempted murder and assault with a deadly weapon. Those charges stemmed from an incident reported on December 1, 2006, when Chang and two associates stabbed a 17-year-old boy during an argument at Sierra Madre's Memorial Park in Los Angeles County. Due to his prior felony status, he was prohibited from possessing weapons or ammunition. However, during the search following this incident, officers found multiple weapons and equipment in Chang's possession, including one firearm with an extended magazine, one semi-automatic 9mm pistol, a ballistic vest, a second handgun, an AR-style rifle, multiple additional magazines, three knives, more than 1,000 rounds of ammunition, and hallucinogenic mushrooms. The female officer seen, a 20-year California Highway Patrol veteran, was shot once in the shoulder by Chang, and was airlifted to the Community Regional Medical Center where she made a full recovery. California Highway Patrol officers were not equipped with body-worn cameras at the time of the incident. However, the agency is in the process of deploying body cameras to all 7,600 patrol officers, with full implementation targeted for March 2006. Chang's personal files and journal entries indicated significant psychological concerns. His writings stated that he was being followed by the feds, and they tried to intimidate him by placing spyware on his phone and firing gunshots near his home. He also wrote that his third eye knows about the Fed's plans, claimed to be the King of Hershey Street, and referenced having a second-degree black belt. On social media, he shared a post stating that he was learning to master self and a community revolution was in progress. During the court trial on July 22, 2004, a jury found Chang guilty of five counts of premeditated and deliberate attempted murder, assault with a semi-automatic firearm on peace officers, being a felon in possession of firearms, ammunition, and a ballistic vest, felony evading, and special allegations related to the discharge of a firearm. In the end, Marvin Joseph Chang was sentenced to 208 years to life in prison, where he will spend the rest of his life. Have you ever wondered why police don't react to gunshots immediately? Well, that's because sometimes the environment lies to your ears. I learned the horror way years ago when I was shot at. And truthfully, the scary part wasn't the gunfire, it was not known where the shots were coming from. Now put yourself in this situation, you're moving, your heartbeat is loud, and the terrain is bending sound in every direction. So you don't hear the gun shots, you hear possibility, and every noise could be nothing or the last warning you get. Then the worst happens, the threat stops moving in front of you, it starts existing somewhere around you. No visual, no direction, just the knowledge that a person with a gun has already decided to use it. Now, I'm almost positive that when those rounds popped off near that female officer, she wasn't thinking about policy. She likely had an adrenaline dump and her body scream to move now. Cover becomes oxygen, distance becomes time, and every step she took was a calculation between freezing and exposing herself. Now, I don't believe she yelled for help because she was panicking. She probably was already shot, and she knew that the isolation, plus the injury is what kills cops. Remember that you're surviving on instinct, hoping that your backup can find you before the shooter finds them. As a cop, you won't always hear the danger coming. You won't always know where it is. And surviving policing sometimes means acting decisively inside uncertainty because waiting for clarity is how officers don't make it home.
